preamble: An onset velar nasal [ŋ] loses its oral closure, leaving its nasality on the following vowel, so that ŋo-type syllables surface with a nasalized [õ] and a glottal or breathy onset. Michaud, Jacques & Rankin (2012) document this onset-to-vowel transfer of nasality as a minority but recurrent pathway, distinct from the far more common loss of a coda nasal. With an [ŋ] source and an [õ] outcome specifically, the evidence is narrow: a single lexical item in one Mon dialect, and a synchronic free variant in two Tamang words.
phoneticEffects: Nasality Transfer, Vowel Nasalization, Loss of Oral Closure

examples.from: ŋoa 'day' (Modern Mon, Shorto 1962: 90; Literary Mon tṅay)
examples.note: Recorded in a Mon dialect on the east bank of the Meklong (Rajburi Province, Photharam District, Thailand) by Christian Bauer in 1978. The devoiced nasal onset lost its oral closure, and its nasality was transferred to the vowel.
Free variation on words with tone 4, where the onset /ŋ/ alternates with breathy [ɦ] and the whole syllable is nasalized (Martine Mazaudon, cited in Michaud et al. 2012).
The same alternation with a high back vowel, the only other word of this shape.

sources: Michaud, A., Jacques, G., & Rankin, R. L. (2012). Historical transfer of nasality between consonantal onset and vowel: From C to V or from V to C? Diachronica, 29(2), 201-230. https://shs.hal.science/halshs-00580260
